title: Pokémon & Monster-Collecting
blurb: The genre that defined the Game Boy Color commercially — Pokémon's second generation, plus the wave of monster-collecting imitators it inspired.
games: The sequel that added a whole new region, a day/night cycle, and breeding, still argued by many longtime fans to be the series' peak.
Adds an animated player sprite and a Suicune-chasing storyline to Gold and Silver's Johto, the definitive way to play the generation.
An entire card game engine translated faithfully into software, complete with AI duelists modeled after in-game gym leaders.

Built on Kirby's Pinball Land's engine, with a built-in Rumble Pak and all 151 original Pokémon to catch mid-flipper-run. Europe's release lagged more than a year behind North America's — the widest gap of any Pokémon title on this list.
A Panel de Pon-engine puzzler reskinned with Pokémon, sharper and faster than its N64 cousin.
Enix's answer to Pokémon, breeding and battling monsters years before “monster tamer” became its own crowded genre.
Splits into two versions like its inspiration, with a deeper breeding system and a much larger monster roster.
The last Game Boy Color game Nintendo ever published, an anime tie-in adventure far more charming than it has any right to be.
A robot-collecting RPG with a battle-and-trade hook nearly identical to Pokémon's, split across Sun and Star versions.

title: Zelda & Nintendo Action-Adventure
blurb: Nintendo's first color Zelda outing anchors a small but essential chapter of first-party handheld adventure design.
games: The Legend of Zelda: Oracle of Seasons
A dungeon-focused Zelda built around season-shifting puzzles, designed to be played as a linked pair with Oracle of Ages.
The Legend of Zelda: Oracle of Ages
The time-travel half of the linked Oracle duology, leaning harder into puzzle logic than combat.
A structurally strange Wario game with no game-over state, where treasure and time-of-day mechanics reshape levels you've already cleared.
A cartridge with a built-in tilt sensor, years before motion controls were a mainstream pitch.
A color remake of the beloved 1990 NES action-RPG, brighter and more legible than the original ever could be.

title: Platformers
blurb: From Rare's prolific Nintendo-published run to WayForward's earliest work, the GBC's platforming chapter is stacked with talent that would define handheld games for a decade after.
games: Released so late in the system's life almost nobody saw it at the time, now considered one of the best-looking games ever squeezed onto the hardware.
The NES original plus Lost Levels, save states, and new challenge modes, built specifically to show off what color added to a classic.
Rare's SNES benchmark compressed into a handheld cart, its pre-rendered look holding up far better than it should on this screen.
The limbless platforming icon's only Game Boy Color outing, built from the ground up rather than ported down.
A methodical puzzle-platformer about a chick collecting eggs with a toolkit of one-use gadgets, years before its celebrated Wii revival.
Remixes stages and bosses from the SNES X games into new handheld-sized levels.
A sequel pulling from X4 and X5, with tighter pacing than the original Xtreme.
A grapple-swinging platformer built by Nintendo's own North American studio under license from Capcom.
A gravity-flipping platformer starring a teenage witch, an early sign of the studio talent that would later make Shantae.
A cutesy, family-friendly prequel to the notoriously crude N64 game, unrecognizable in tone from what Conker would become.
Digital Eclipse's first wholly original game rather than a port, built in a famously tight three-month turnaround.

title: Sports
blurb: Nintendo's own handheld-companion sports duo headlines a chapter of games built as their own thing, not console ports squeezed down.
games: A companion to the N64 game with its own characters and courses, not a stripped-down port.
Same handheld-companion approach as Mario Golf, deep enough that its RPG-lite training mode became a fan favorite in its own right.
A streetball-style three-on-three game built specifically for the handheld rather than downsized from a console original.
A separately-built handheld entry in Acclaim's baseball series, developed apart from its console namesake.
Arcade two-on-two basketball with the series' signature exaggerated dunks, shrunk down without losing its over-the-top energy.
A GBC launch-window title that keeps ten-pin bowling's rhythm intact despite the tiny screen.

title: Racing
blurb: Five ways to go fast, from a Disney-branded kart racer to a rally sim ported down from PC and PS1.
games: A rally racer built around Infogrames' PC/console series, released in Europe as V-Rally: Championship Edition.
A kart racer starring Mickey Mouse, built by Rare during their prolific late-90s Nintendo-published handheld run.
A handheld entry in the off-road racing series, developed in-house alongside its PC and PS1 versions. Rebranded entirely for its European release the following spring, as 4x4 World Trophy.
A stunt-driving racer with looping, ramp-heavy tracks built for one-more-run replay value.
A Europe-only motocross racer that never crossed the Atlantic.

title: Fighting & Action
blurb: Stealth, survival horror, and one very famous case of a handheld game trading on a name that wasn't quite its own.
games: A single-player-only conversion of the arcade fighter, without link-cable versus but with the full roster and move sets intact.

Released in the West simply as “Metal Gear Solid” to trade on the PS1 game's name, this is actually a wholly separate, original stealth game built for the handheld. The Japanese and European cartridges also included a bonus in-game radio broadcast that Konami quietly cut from the North American release.
A top-down action game bearing the N64 shooter's name and characters but built as its own distinct handheld experience.
A side-scrolling action game starring the one-liner-spouting mercenary, trading first-person shooting for run-and-gun platforming.

An overhead survival-horror hybrid with first-person shooting segments, developed under story input from series creator Shinji Mikami. An unusual release order for the era: Europe actually got it first, months ahead of both Japan and North America.
Alone in the Dark: The New Nightmare
A from-scratch handheld build of the survival-horror series, developed separately from the console/PC version by the same publisher.

The infamously troubled PC shooter's handheld spinoff plays it as a straightforward action game, and quietly outshines its console namesake's reputation. Europe got the only proper retail release anywhere in the world; Japan's release came a year later only through a Nintendo Power download kiosk, and North America's version was cancelled outright.

title: Puzzle
blurb: Falling blocks, popping bubbles, and one very literal exercise in digging straight down.
games: The GBC launch-window Tetris, adding color-coded pieces and a genuinely useful multiplayer mode.
Dig straight down through color-coded blocks without getting crushed, a perfect one-handed handheld translation of the arcade original.
An action-RPG spin on Bomberman rather than the usual multiplayer bomb-em-up, closer to a Zelda-style dungeon crawl.
A GBC-launch color re-release of a 1997 monochrome Bomberman puzzle-platformer built by the series' own developer.

An obscure falling-jewel puzzler from Taito's deep catalog, rarely mentioned outside dedicated puzzle-genre roundups. A planned North American release was cancelled outright; Europe got it anyway, over a year later in December 2000.
A bubble-popping puzzler entry that adds new modes on top of the core Puzzle Bobble formula.
A hexagonal tile-matching puzzler developed differently for its Japanese and North American releases.

title: Strategy & Simulation
blurb: An unlikely run of real-time and turn-based strategy experiments, anchored by three generations of a beloved farming sim.
games: A real-time strategy game in the Warcraft mold, widely considered proof the genre could actually work on a D-pad.
A modern military RTS ported down from PC, commanding armored units across a simplified but genuine strategy layer.
A Japan-only turn-based wargame in the Famicom Wars lineage, the same design DNA that would become Advance Wars.
A late Japan-only sequel refining the series' turn-based unit combat.
A from-scratch handheld build of the artillery-combat series, developed separately from Team17's console and PC versions.

A card-battle RPG hybrid built around the anime's dueling rules, deep enough to satisfy players who skipped the trading cards entirely. Europe didn't get its own release until a full year later, in 2003.
Heroes of Might and Magic II
A surprisingly faithful handheld adaptation of the PC turn-based strategy classic.
A distinct, from-scratch color entry in the farming-sim series, not a port of the earlier monochrome Harvest Moon.
Expands the farm-sim formula with new crops, animals, and a bigger town to build relationships in.
The trilogy's close, refining pacing and social systems built up over the two previous entries.

title: Role-Playing Adventures
blurb: Square's absence is filled by Enix, Atlus, and Namco — a deep RPG chapter that leans heavily on Japan-only side stories that never made the trip West.
games: Faithful color remakes of the two Famicom games that started the entire JRPG genre in Japan.
A remake of the NES-era game many consider the series' best pre-SNES entry, now with a party-swapping class system intact.
A prequel built around randomized dungeons and a heavier strategy layer than the SNES originals it follows.
Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone

A turn-based RPG adaptation of the first book, wandering Hogwarts and casting spells in a distinctly Final Fantasy-influenced structure. Released the same day in Europe under the book's original title there: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone.
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets
A direct sequel expanding the first game's spellcasting and exploration systems.
A fishing RPG that plays it surprisingly straight, with real tackle strategy layered under its cute exterior. Europe waited over a year for its own release, arriving in December 2000.
A sequel with multiple playable characters and an expanded fishing-and-story loop.
A roguelike dungeon-crawler with monster-taming and tower-building layered on top, adapted from the PS1 original.
A Western localization of a 1992 Japanese Megami Tensei spin-off, effectively the first color RPG Atlus brought to North America.
A Japan-only spin-off letting players cosplay as any recruited character, spun off from Namco's original Tales RPG.
Shin Megami Tensei: Devil Children — Black/Red/White Book
A Japan-only monster-fusion RPG trilogy that predates the Devil Children franchise's later GBA and anime expansion.
A Japan-only side story spun off from the acclaimed PS1 RPG, built as an original handheld adventure rather than a port.

title: Shooters & Arcade Classics
blurb: Arcade history in color — three of Namco and Taito's oldest hits, plus a shooter compilation and two late-system deep cuts.
games: A two-in-one color compilation of R-Type and R-Type II, the definitive way to play either on original hardware.
A single-player-only color conversion of the arcade original, stripped of its multiplayer but faithful to the core invasion loop.
A GBC-launch-era conversion of the arcade classic that reintroduced an entire generation to hopping across traffic.
A color-enhanced handheld port that keeps the harder, more randomized ghost AI that made the arcade sequel tougher than the original.
The arcade original in color, maze layout and ghost patterns untouched by four decades of imitators.
A vertical shooter with smooth scrolling and multiple weapon loadouts, released late and quietly in the system's final year.
Play a giant monster smashing city blocks, with the series' co-op destruction intact even at handheld scale.

title: Licensed & Movie Tie-Ins
blurb: The GBC's shovelware reputation came from somewhere — but a handful of licensed tie-ins here are genuinely well-built, not just cash-grabs.
games: A top-down reimagining of Lara Croft's exploration-and-puzzle formula, built to work without a 3D camera. Titled simply Tomb Raider in Europe, where North America's box added Starring Lara Croft.
An unusually well-regarded licensed platformer that lets the show's spoiled antagonist headline her own adventure.
Austin Powers: Oh, Behave! and Welcome to My Underground Lair!
A two-cartridge tie-in split between hero and villain campaigns, published in North America by an unlikely source: Rockstar Games.
Dragon Ball Z: Legendary Super Warriors
A one-on-one fighter with a huge roster spanning the anime's Saiyan through Buu arcs.
Action Man: Search for Base X
A toy-line tie-in action-adventure with more genuine level design than most licensed platformers of its era.
A top-down rescue-vehicle action game built around the toy brand rather than a racing game, despite the name.
A handheld reimagining of the 3D platformer's sequel, rebuilt from the ground up for two dimensions.

title: Cult Classics & Japan-Only Curios
blurb: The deepest cuts in the whole collection — including a near-unbroken run of games that never left Japan at all.
games: Classic Game & Watch toys reimagined with both their original look and a “modern” reskinned mode, now finally in color.
A third helping of remastered Game & Watch classics, including Donkey Kong Jr. and Mario's Cement Factory.
Known in Japan as Elemental Tale, an overlooked action-RPG about a boy solving elemental puzzles across a fantasy world.
Bomberman Max: Blue Champion / Red Challenger

A pair of connectable Bomberman versions blending the series' puzzle-action with light RPG progression — titled Hero of Light and Warrior of Darkness in Japan, entirely different names again from their North American release.

A Japan-and-Europe-only compilation cartridge that finally brought Game Boy Color support to a set of Konami's earlier monochrome classics — never released in North America. The European cut also quietly reshuffled the Japanese lineup and swapped one Japan-specific mascot on the menu for the more internationally familiar Penta from Antarctic Adventure.
A desert-island survival game about foraging, crafting, and staying alive with almost no combat at all. Released in Europe several months later under a different name: Stranded Kids.
A Japan-only port of a beloved 1991 TurboGrafx-16 shooter, a genuine deep-cut for import shoot-em-up collectors.
An action-puzzle spin-off of Tecmo's monster-raising series, built more like a puzzle-platformer than its console cousins.
A side-scrolling ninja action game with a heavier emphasis on stealth than most genre peers of its era.
A Japan-only tactical RPG from the developer who would go on to make Mario & Luigi: Superstar Saga.
Kettō Transformers Beast Wars: Beast Senshi Saikyō Kettei-sen
A Japan-only Transformers fighting game tied to the Beast Wars toy and cartoon line.
From TV Animation One Piece: Maboroshi no Grand Line Boukenhen!
A Japan-only One Piece adventure game from early in the anime's handheld-game history.
Daiku no Gen-san: Kachikachi no Tonkachi ga Kachi
A Japan-only spin-off of Irem's carpenter-hero Hammerin' Harry series, built as an action-puzzle game.
Meitantei Conan: Karakuri Jiin Satsujin Jiken
A Japan-only Detective Conan mystery-adventure, investigating a murder in a trap-filled temple.
